source.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
source.authors: Minyoung Huh; Brian Cheung; Tongzhou Wang; Phillip Isola

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests representational convergence with its own mutual-nearest-neighbor measurements across vision models and across paired vision-language inputs, including scale/performance and metric-sensitivity analyses. It is an original source, not a reproduction of an earlier study.
record.gate_note: The paper also surveys stitching, seed convergence, neurons, and other alignment findings, but those cited results are not rows. The paper's own results include vision-model alignment by transfer competence, cross-modal alignment, alternative metrics and settings, and caption-density comparisons. Aggregate figure trends are recorded where the text describes them; individual plotted points without reliably stated values are not assigned to named checkpoints.
record.test_reason: This is the original source for V1/V2 (the Platonic Representation Hypothesis). Its own mutual-kNN experiments define the method and measure: 78 vision models binned by VTAB competence, and LLM–vision alignment on WIT image-caption pairs. It also runs metric, k and caption-density analyses bearing on V6/V7. Because it is an original source, no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that alignment rises with competence and scale, within vision and across vision and language. They hypothesize convergence toward a shared statistical model of reality, formalized for contrastive learners as a PMI kernel. They acknowledge that alignment is incomplete (0.16), depends on the metric and on caption information content, and may not hold for special-purpose systems or for modalities carrying different information.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops and uses mutual-nearest-neighbor alignment, paired-image-caption comparisons, and metric-sensitivity analyses to test its own hypothesis; this is the original source rather than a reproduction of the other cited source.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment trends vary with metric and nearest-neighbor count; the paper reports weaker or less conclusive trends for CKA/high k and stronger local trends at lower k. Cross-modal alignment also varies with vision-model training task, explicit language supervision, ImageNet fine-tuning, and caption density.
record.problems: Cross-modal maximum reported alignment is only 0.16 on a metric with theoretical maximum 1, and the authors say the significance of the remaining gap is unresolved. The principal cross-modal results rely on one paired image-caption dataset and mutual-nearest-neighbor-style measures; the paper itself shows metric and setting sensitivity. Many plotted results are not numerically described in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's numerous per-checkpoint curves in Figures 3, 13, and 14 are not given as textual numbers and could not be reliably assigned to individual model checkpoints from the flattened figure text; aggregate trends and explicit setting effects are retained instead. Surveyed results from cited papers are excluded.

untested.parts: Seed or initialization convergence is only cited (Ainsworth et al., mode connectivity); no experiment.
Stitching, linear maps, relative representations and unpaired mapping are cited only.
Rosetta neurons and shared features are cited only.
No test of a plateau. No experiment separating shared data or objectives from a common model of reality.
No same-family size sweep within the vision-vision analysis. Competence bins, not parameter counts, are the axis.

missing.what: Taking the last LLM token showed no strong alignment signal. Prompted last-token features gave similar trends but slightly lower scores. Alignment is reported as the maximum over layer pairs. All of this shows dependence on the choice of representation.
Color case study: PMI-based color embeddings from CIFAR-10 pixel co-occurrence and from SimCSE/RoBERTa roughly recover the CIELAB perceptual layout. The comparison is qualitative only.

record.verdict_notes: The study is an original source, so verdict labels are withheld for all versions. Tranche is set to T1 because the study defines the original method and measure. Most results are figure-only aggregates. Rows R6–R10 are the paper's own sensitivity analyses, and they bear on V6 as a challenge to the paper's own main measure.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments do not comprehensively compare independent models spanning all possible architectures, objectives, datasets, and modalities, or establish an endpoint across future scales.
The cross-modal experiment uses paired Wikipedia images and captions; it does not test all modalities or establish that every vision and language model family improves monotonically.
Same-architecture convergence across random initializations and shared subspaces is discussed through cited work, not tested in the paper's experiments.
Linear maps, stitching, relative representations, and unpaired mappings are discussed or cited, not tested in the paper's own experiments.
Recurring interpretable neurons or features are mentioned through cited work, not tested in the paper's experiments.
The paper varies alignment metric and nearest-neighbor settings, and varies caption density, but does not systematically test out-of-distribution inputs.

The paper reports incomplete alignment and effects associated with explicit language supervision and fine-tuning. It does not establish that shared training data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause the measured alignment, nor does it establish a plateau.

rows.subject: 78 vision models (aggregate within-performance bins)
rows.size_stated: varied; model-by-model sizes not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Measured average within-bin representation alignment and related it to transfer-task competence.

conditions.value: Places-365 validation images for alignment; VTAB for competence
bins by percentage of VTAB tasks solved

rows.measure: Average intra-bin mutual-nearest-neighbor alignment versus percentage of VTAB tasks solved.
rows.value: Figure 2 reports that higher-competence bins are more aligned; numerical bin values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error shown in Figure 2; values not stated in text.
rows.note: The paper reports this as an aggregate over 78 models; it defines a solved task as performance at least 80% of the best among the 78 models.

relation.reason: Its own experiments measure competence-related alignment within vision and across vision and language, with metric and caption-density analyses.

tranche.reason: This original source defines and applies the mutual-nearest-neighbor method and measure used as the baseline.

source_check.notes: Cross-modal scores maximize over layer comparisons, including concatenated features; last-token representations alone showed no strong alignment. Statements were checked only for their claims about this study; no verdicts are listed for this original source.
